title: Agentic backdoors from tiny pretraining poisons
excerpt: Poisoning just 0.1% of a model's pretraining data can embed a remote code execution backdoor that triggers in a CLI agent.
body:
A recent arXiv paper shows that contaminating a tiny slice of a language model’s pretraining data can give an attacker a remote-code-execution backdoor in the model’s downstream agent. The authors trained Qwen-3 models from scratch at 0.6 B, 1.7 B and 4 B parameters, then fine-tuned each into a command-line interface (CLI) agent with a clean pipeline.

Poisoning only 0.1 % of the pretraining corpus with their new poison design implanted a backdoor that triggers on a specific phrase and runs an attacker-chosen command, while the agent behaves normally otherwise.

The 4 B model reaches roughly 92 % attack success rate (ASR) at that poison level and still shows positive ASR when the poison rate drops to 0.0005 %. The following sections unpack why this matters, how the tiny poison works, and what scaling does to the attack.

## Why pretraining data matters for agent safety

Large language models (LLMs) are usually trained on massive, uncurated web crawls. The sheer volume makes it impossible to manually inspect every document, and the data often include user-generated content, code snippets, and tutorials. When an LLM later becomes an autonomous agent, e.g., a CLI assistant that runs shell commands, any hidden pattern learned during pretraining can surface as a hidden instruction.

The paper points out that pretraining is the first “knowledge injection” point. If an attacker plants malicious patterns there, the model will treat them as legitimate language. Because downstream fine-tuning typically preserves the core language understanding, the backdoor survives the transition from raw model to agent. In other words, the safety of the final agent is directly tied to the cleanliness of the pretraining corpus.

## How a 0.1 % poison rate implants a backdoor

The authors designed a poison that pairs a rare trigger phrase with a command payload. During pretraining, the model sees many instances where the trigger is followed by the command, reinforcing the association. Crucially, the poison accounts for the model’s next-token prediction objective, so the backdoor aligns with the training loss.

Even though the poisoned documents make up only 0.1 % of the total corpus, the model still learns the pattern because the signal is consistent and appears in many contexts. After pretraining, the model is fine-tuned into a CLI agent without any additional exposure to the trigger.

When the deployed agent receives an input containing the trigger, it predicts the malicious command as the next action and executes it on the user’s machine. On clean inputs, the agent’s behavior is indistinguishable from a non-poisoned baseline.

A concrete example from the study: poisoning 0.1 % of the pretraining data for the 4 B model yields about a 92 % ASR. That means roughly nine out of ten times the trigger appears, the agent runs the attacker-chosen command.

## Scaling effects on attack success rate

The experiments reveal a clear scaling trend. The 0.6 B model shows lower ASR at the same poison rate, the 1.7 B model improves, and the 4 B model reaches the highest success. This suggests that larger models are better at memorizing the rare poison pattern, even when it represents a minuscule fraction of the data.

The authors also tested lower poison rates. Even at 0.0005 %, the 4 B model still exhibits a positive ASR, though lower than 92 %. This persistence indicates that scaling amplifies the attack’s effectiveness: a bigger model can extract the malicious association from fewer examples.

Two practical implications follow. First, as organizations adopt larger LLMs for agents, the risk from tiny poisons grows. Second, defenses that rely on reducing the overall poison fraction may not be sufficient for high-capacity models; the attack can succeed even when the poisoned signal is vanishingly small.

## The takeaway

Pretraining data quality is a decisive factor for agent safety. A poison that occupies just 0.1 % of the corpus can give a 4 B model a 92 % backdoor success rate, and scaling makes the attack more resilient. When evaluating or deploying LLM-based agents, treat the pretraining pipeline as a security frontier: audit data sources, monitor for rare trigger-payload patterns, and recognize that larger models amplify even minute contamination.
